Rhinoform: A Limitation-Aware Interactive Platform for Sparse-Control Nasal Morphology Preview on Registered 3D Face Meshes
Final-Year Individual Project
Department of Computing
A Limitation-Aware Interactive Platform for 0.16cm Sparse-Control Nasal Morphology Preview 0.16cm on Registered 3D Face Meshes
From a controlled sparse-control dense-deformation benchmark to a conservative and auditable research prototype for morphology communication

Author: Li Zequan \\[0.45em] Supervisor: Dr Jiankang Deng \\[0.45em] Programme: MEng Electronic and Information Engineering \\[0.45em] Department: Department of Computing \\[0.45em] Institution: Imperial College London
Rhinoplasty has a comparatively high revision rate, and dissatisfaction with postoperative nasal appearance is a major reason patients seek revision.
A key contributor is inadequate preoperative communication, which can leave the patient and surgeon expecting different results .
Three-dimensional preoperative preview can make the intended change easier to discuss .
This dissertation separates two technical requirements for such a preview: fidelity to the registered target morphology and regularity of the predicted surface.

On the registered FaceScape topology, this dissertation formulates the problem as source-conditioned sparse-control morphology completion: given the displacements of nine FaceScape-calibrated semantic nasal landmarks and a source identity, the goal is to predict the dense displacement field of a 3934-vertex nasal ROI.
Eight methods are evaluated under the same identity-disjoint protocol, using the same 9\,900 test pairs, sparse controls, and metrics.

Within this benchmark, the proposed certified RB-SR is compared with three geometric methods (Laplacian, bi-Laplacian and As-Rigid-As-Possible deformation), two learned methods (CVAE and LAMM), and one statistical method (the source-PCA Ridge anchor).
A fixed Ridge--CVAE hybrid is included only as a matched internal ablation.
RB-SR admits a spatially gated neural residual on top of the Ridge anchor and then projects it so that its folded faces are a subset of the anchor's.
Evaluation measures dense fidelity with free-ROI RMSE and surface regularity with target-relative new normal flips and edge-strain p_95.

Certified RB-SR improves its matched ridge anchor on both predeclared primary outcomes (ROI RMSE -1.30\%, new flips -31.6\%, both Holm-significant across 100 test identities) with no detected edge-strain cost, and certifies all 9\,900 test pairs while retaining 99.2\% of the admitted residual.

No single method dominates the study: LAMM attains the lowest reconstruction error, ARAP the best geometric regularity, and certified RB-SR the best-justified operating point between them---more regular than LAMM (74\% fewer new flips, 36\% lower edge strain) and more accurate than every geometric editor.

A post-hoc higher-capacity configuration of the same family surpasses LAMM on all three metrics, indicating that the operating point reflects a deliberate conservative choice rather than a capacity ceiling.
The deployed prototype treats this evidence as a risk--utility operating point.

The ridge anchor answers every control movement in real time, while the certified residual is computed asynchronously and replaces the anchor only when its fold-subset certificate holds; requests outside the evaluated control range are scaled back or withheld by a separate input-applicability policy.
The released browser build is locked to the released assets and passes 51 automated checks against stored reference goldens.
Its scope is morphology communication on a registered surface mesh; it makes no surgical-outcome, airway, or cross-dataset claim.

Rhinoplasty occupies an unusual position among surgical procedures.

It is technically demanding and one of the most frequently performed facial aesthetic operations, yet it also carries one of the lowest satisfaction rates and one of the highest revision rates of any cosmetic procedure.
Reported revision rates cluster consistently between 5\% and 15\% across independent series , and crucially the dominant reason patients return is rarely a threat to safety or breathing.

In a single-centre study of 732 closed rhinoplasties, the surgical revision rate was 8.6\%, and the factors most strongly associated with revision were morphological---wide or deviated noses and residual contour irregularities---rather than acute complications .

A recent literature synthesis of 40 studies reaches the same conclusion from the patient side: the majority of structural complaints driving dissatisfaction are a residual dorsal hump (\( 20\%\) of patients) and persistent nasal-tip fullness or irregularity (\(19\%\)--\(37\%\)) .
The deeper pattern in this literature is that dissatisfaction is frequently an expectation problem rather than an execution problem.

The same synthesis identifies ``ineffective patient--provider communication'', inadequate informed consent, and a failure to reach an explicit consensus on surgical goals as recurring, modifiable contributors to postoperative dissatisfaction .
In other words, the surgeon's internal plan and the picture in the patient's mind are often two different noses, and the gap only becomes visible after the cast comes off.
For a patient this can feel like opening a blind box; for a surgeon it is a documentation and medico-legal liability.
A natural remedy is to make the intended change visible and discussable before surgery.
The clinical evidence here is encouraging.

Preoperative computer imaging is associated with significantly improved patient-reported benefit , and three-dimensional simulation is now the preferred consultation aid where it is available: in a series of 172 consecutive candidates, 95\% considered 3D morphing an added value over 2D, and 84\% of revision patients said 3D simulation helped them understand the aims of surgery (versus 61\% for primary patients) .
More recent work using a commercial 3D platform reports that simulation accuracy correlates strongly with eventual satisfaction ( = 0.66, P < .001) .
Simulation, done well, aligns expectations and supports shared decision-making.
The value of a three-dimensional consultation tool is not only that it shows a nose more vividly than a two-dimensional photograph.
It also makes the design face-specific.
Patients often arrive with a desired aesthetic reference: a celebrity nose, a filtered image, or an idealised mental picture of a high bridge, projected tip or narrow alar base.
The difficult question is not whether that nose is attractive in isolation, but whether it belongs on this face, with this radix, dorsum, tip support, alar width and surrounding facial proportions.

A personalised 3D preview can therefore redirect the consultation from ``can I have that nose?'' to ``what version of that intention is coherent on my face?'' This is a communication benefit that generic 2D morphing and celebrity-reference discussion cannot provide.

Rhinoform replaces free-form verbal negotiation with nine sparse handles on the nasal ROI; a dense deformation is completed automatically and every accepted edit carries a hard fold certificate.
The system is a communication aid, not a surgical prediction.

An effective preview must therefore translate verbal preferences, such as ``raising the nasal tip slightly'' or ``narrowing the dorsum'', into a concrete shape proposal that can be adjusted, inspected from multiple angles and discussed against the patient's own face.

This creates a second obligation: the same visual persuasiveness that helps communication can also raise unrealistic expectations , especially when counselling is not supported by a concrete visual anchor .
Rhinoform is positioned accordingly as a morphology-communication prototype for plan comparison, interactive adjustment and expectation alignment.
This framing is summarised in .
This is also where safety enters the consultation.

Some desired noses are not merely aesthetically mismatched but outside a reasonable deformation envelope: the requested bridge may be too high for the starting anatomy, the projected tip may require excessive surface stretch, or the alar narrowing may create a locally folded surface in the mesh.
Rhinoform treats these cases as out-of-distribution or high-risk proposals to be discussed, shrunk or refused, rather than as images to render persuasively.

The goal is to help the patient and clinician converge toward an individually suitable design before surgery, not to help the patient demand an idealised geometry that is incompatible with their own face.
To study previewing rigorously rather than anecdotally, the consultation gesture is reduced to a controlled geometric task on registered 3D face meshes.
A surgeon or patient expresses a desired change through a small number of semantic handles on the nose---raise the radix, lower the dorsal hump, rotate or deproject the tip, narrow the alar base.
Concretely, the system is driven by nine nasal landmarks whose 3D displacements form a 27-dimensional control vector.

The task is to turn that sparse intent into a dense displacement field over a nasal region of interest (ROI) of 3934 vertices on a topologically consistent mesh, so that the rest of the nose follows the handles in a coherent way.
The application boundary follows from the same clinical evidence.

The editable object is deliberately restricted to the nasal ROI, because the motivating complaints concentrate on radix, dorsum, tip and alar morphology; the surrounding full head is rendered so the preview can be judged in facial context.
A realistic full-face render is therefore contextual display, while the technical claim remains nasal surface morphology within the registered ROI.
This is a genuinely hard, under-determined inverse problem: nine handles cannot uniquely determine thousands of vertices, so infinitely many dense fields are consistent with the same control input.

The central difficulty---and the reason a naive editor is dangerous in a consultation---is that many of those solutions are visually plausible but geometrically degenerate: surfaces that self-intersect, flip their normals, or stretch local triangles beyond what real nasal morphology supports.
A preview tool that silently displays such an artefact as a confident ``after'' image is actively misleading.
The technical contribution is a dense predictor with an explicit trust boundary: the system estimates the nasal response and reports when the estimate leaves the benchmarked geometric regime.
Source identity conditioning supplies the first part of that boundary.
The statistical backbone conditions the sparse-to-dense prediction on the starting facial geometry, so the same landmark request can expand differently on different registered noses.
The live control-scale applicability check flags requests outside the evaluated control range and can scale them back or withhold them.

Normal flips and edge strain are shown separately as descriptive geometric read-outs: edge strain is a surface-stretch proxy relevant to skin-envelope tension, and normal flips are a proxy for local fold-over or surface collapse.
The fold certificate, rather than either read-out, controls admission of the learned residual.
The full tensor contract and gating mechanism are formalised in .
The project follows an applied-systems logic: pain point first, then concrete requirements, then a prototype whose behaviour can be measured.

The dissertation is organised around four research questions that connect the software system to the method and then to the evaluation evidence:

Under a single fixed protocol---registered FaceScape topology, a nine-landmark sparse-control interface, and identity-level evaluation---which deformation prior best completes a sparse nasal edit into a dense displacement field: classical geometric editors, a source-conditioned statistical anchor, a neural generator, a strong external learned baseline (LAMM), or the proposed certified RB-SR framework?

Does certified RB-SR improve its matched ridge anchor under predeclared, Holm-corrected primary outcomes, and---once the stronger baselines are included---where does it sit on the resulting accuracy--regularity trade-off?
Is that trade-off a capacity ceiling of the method family, or a deliberate choice of operating point?
Which components do the work?

What do the component chain (anchor, residual proposal, learned gate, hard certificate) and the source-conditioning ablation reveal about where the accuracy gain comes from and why a hard admission stage is necessary?

How should this evidence be translated into a user-facing consultation prototype that exposes the credibility and failure modes of each preview---and what do regional, noise, failure-case and conformance diagnostics reveal about the limits of the deployed system?
In answering these questions, this dissertation makes four contributions:

A unified sparse-control, dense-deformation benchmark for nasal morphology on registered FaceScape topology, with an identity-disjoint split, a fixed nine-landmark control protocol, a strict free-vertex scorer, and a reproducible evaluation harness.

Eight methods---classical geometric editors (Laplacian, bi-Laplacian, ARAP), a source-PCA ridge anchor, a CVAE generator, a fixed hybrid, the strong external learned baseline LAMM (retrained and adapted to the same protocol in response to examiner feedback), and the proposed certified RB-SR---are scored on the same 9\,900 held-out identity pairs under identical conditions, which is what makes the comparison meaningful.
The certified RB-SR framework.

A source-conditioned ridge anchor supplies a stable sparse-to-dense backbone; a CVAE proposes a dense correction; a learned per-vertex gate admits the residual spatially; and a hard ridge-relative fold certificate projects the admitted residual so that its folded faces are a subset of the anchor's.

The certificate is motivated by a negative result: no soft-gated configuration satisfied both geometric budgets, so the deployment contract is provided by an explicit projection rather than by optimisation pressure alone.
A statistically disciplined evidence chain.

Predeclared primary outcomes with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Holm correction at identity level, source- and target-clustered sensitivity intervals, a validation-only component chain, a source-conditioning ablation, post-hoc regional, noise and deterministic qualitative diagnostics (including a mandatory failure case), and an explicitly post-hoc capacity study that separates the deployed operating point from the family's accuracy ceiling.
Rhinoform, an interactive 3D consultation prototype that turns the benchmark findings into a working, measured system.

The platform uses the source-conditioned ridge anchor as its real-time default predictor, computes the certified residual asynchronously and admits it only when the fold-subset certificate holds, and scales back or withholds requests outside the evaluated control range via a separate input-applicability policy.
The released browser build is locked to the released assets and passes 51 automated checks against stored reference goldens.

The prototype is the deployed form of the dissertation's empirical finding: a useful morphology preview should combine source-conditioned dense response with explicit, mechanically separated admission guarantees.
Rhinoform is developed as a technical prototype for preoperative morphology communication.
Its purpose is to help patients and surgeons explore face-specific nasal shape changes in 3D, compare alternative editing directions, and discuss expectations using a shared visual reference.
It is not intended to predict the final surgical result.
The claims of this dissertation are therefore limited to the controlled setting in which the system is built and evaluated.
In particular, the system:

predicts geometric nasal shape variation, not surgical outcome, healing, soft-tissue biomechanics, or airway function---in particular, the cross-identity target pairs used for supervision define a benchmark ground truth, not a postoperative state of the source person; is evaluated on a single neutral-expression FaceScape-registered topology, and does not claim cross-dataset or cross-expression generalisation; is evaluated on an internal held-out identity split that was excluded from all final retraining but is not a historically untouched external test set, so the headline results are internal confirmatory evidence rather than external validation; reports deformation magnitudes in uncalibrated FaceScape units rather than physical millimetres, so the values should be interpreted comparatively rather than clinically; is a consultation-support prototype, not a medical device, and is designed to support clinical judgement rather than replace it.
As discusses, many existing rhinoplasty visualisation tools focus on producing a convincing simulated appearance.

This dissertation takes a narrower, accountable route: a controlled sparse-to-dense benchmark becomes an interactive 3D preview system whose behaviour, reliability range, and geometric risks can be explicitly inspected.
The clinical motivation in establishes why shared 3D preview matters.
The related-work task is now more specific: identify the domain measurement concepts a trustworthy preview must respect and use them to evaluate the technical families that could support Rhinoform.
Speaking precisely about ``the nose'' requires fixing its anatomical vocabulary.

Morphologically the nose decomposes into a small set of sub-units---the root, the dorsum, the tip, and the left and right alar regions---and the morphology that drives revision concentrates on exactly these regions ().

This decomposition becomes the partition on which this project both names its interface controls and reports its error, so that where a preview is credible can be read off per sub-unit rather than hidden inside a single aggregate.
The sub-unit surface is not free to move arbitrarily, because it is covered by a skin--soft-tissue envelope with well-characterised mechanics.
A convenient way to make ``over-stretch'' precise is the engineering strain of a surface edge: for a mesh edge e with rest length _e^0 and deformed length _e,
the local fractional change in edge length.

This quantity is clinically loaded because skin does not stretch linearly: its stress--strain response is J-shaped, with a compliant low-strain ``toe'' region followed by a steep rise once the collagen network engages .

Small edits therefore cost little tension, but beyond a threshold the envelope resists sharply, and an operative envelope that is thick, scarred or already under tension has far less margin to redrape over a large local strain; excessive tension can also compromise the soft-tissue conditions on which redraping depends .

It should be stressed that, because this project has no access to skin thickness, cartilage, CT or patient-specific material parameters, edge strain is used here strictly as a geometric proxy for local surface stretch, not as a patient-specific biomechanical estimate.

A preview that silently drives large local surface stretch is thus geometrically implausible and worth flagging---which is the domain rationale for treating Equation eq:edge-strain as a risk signal to be capped, shrunk or refused () rather than rendered persuasively.
Making ``measurable'' operational presupposes a registered 3D representation, in which a vertex index refers to the same anatomical point across every identity.

Only under this condition do both dense per-vertex error and the edge strain of Equation eq:edge-strain become exact quantities computed by direct index correspondence, rather than approximate surface-matching estimates; registration is therefore the precondition for the controlled benchmark and the risk metrics used throughout, and it is what the FaceScape substrate () supplies.

Taken together, this clinical framing distils into the three requirements that the remainder of the chapter evaluates all prior work against: (i) registered locality---local nasal edits on a mesh that preserves anatomical correspondence; (ii) interpretable sparse control---deformation driven by a few intuitive handles rather than global parameters; and (iii) live geometric safety---a result regular enough to be shown in real time, and measurable enough (via strain and normal-flip proxies) that an edit leaving the benchmarked envelope can be quantified and refused.
Every family of methods surveyed below is judged by how well it meets, or fails to meet, these three requirements.

The task is under-determined by construction.
The 27 sparse-control scalars cannot uniquely determine the 11,802 dense displacement unknowns of the 3934-vertex ROI, so infinitely many dense fields are consistent with the same control input.

Every method must therefore supply a prior that decides how the unconstrained vertices move: it is the prior, not the handles, that fills the gap between a few controls and thousands of coordinated vertices.
This is why a preview can look confident yet be untrustworthy---two methods can honour the identical nine handles while disagreeing completely on the surface between them.

The central question of this dissertation is therefore not whether to interpolate but which prior to trust: a generic smoothness prior (geometry-based), a learned population prior (learning-based), or a hybrid that anchors a learned correction to a statistical backbone.

Framing the task this way makes the survey directly comparable---the geometry-based methods of and the learning-based methods of are simply different answers to the same interpolation problem, and can be scored on the same two axes: reconstruction accuracy (how close the dense field is to the held-out FaceScape dense target) and geometric regularity (how free the result is of folds and excess strain).

The one sparse-to-dense task branches into a data-agnostic geometry-based family (Laplacian, bi-Laplacian, ARAP and RBF interpolation), a data-aware learning-based family (VAE/CVAE and mesh autoencoders), and the anchored hybrid this project proposes.

Each branch is a different answer to ``which prior?'', and the taxonomy fixes where every subsequent section sits: covers the statistical backbone the hybrid anchors to, the geometric branch, the learned branch, and the closing synthesis explains why Rhinoform commits to the hybrid branch rather than to either classical extreme.
The statistical backbone that the hybrid branch anchors to comprises the registered face representations on the data-aware branch of .

All of these representations share the registered property whose measurement consequences already established: every face is expressed on a shared mesh topology, so a vertex index refers to the same anatomical point across identities.

This section introduces the statistical representations that the project either builds on or contrasts with---the 3D Morphable Model, its PCA shape space, FLAME, and FaceScape---and clarifies why their global face-space strengths must be repurposed for local, sparse-control nasal editing.
The 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) is the foundational statistical face representation and is a load-bearing reference for this project.
As shows, a 3DMM is learned by densely registering a database of 3D scans and running principal component analysis (PCA) separately on the concatenated vertex coordinates and per-vertex colour.

The result is a low-dimensional generative space: any face can be written as a mean shape s plus a linear combination of orthonormal shape eigenvectors u_j weighted by coefficients , \[ s( ) = s+ _j _ju_j, \] with an analogous texture model.
Walking a single coefficient along traverses one interpretable mode of population variation (), and the model is fitted to a 2D image by analysis-by-synthesis ().
The key property Rhinoform inherits is the statistical coordinate system that PCA provides.
PCA converts a raw high-dimensional vertex set into a compact, data-aware representation of population variation.
Its key limitation, however, is equally important: classic 3DMM edits are global and linear, whereas this dissertation targets local, handle-driven nasal deformation.
Rhinoform therefore adopts the PCA-space idea without adopting global coefficient editing as the interaction mechanism.
In other words, it reuses the statistical space as a source-conditioned anchor, but replaces global PCA manipulation with sparse local control over the nasal ROI.

Expression-aware models extend this statistical face-space tradition.
FLAME factorises a head into interpretable parameter groups---identity shape , expression and pose ---combined through learned blendshapes and linear blend skinning around an articulated skeleton ().

Its inputs are the parameter vectors; its output is a posed full-head mesh; and its key modules are the shape/expression PCA blendshapes and the jaw, neck and eye joints that make expression and articulation physically plausible ().

In the taxonomy of this chapter, FLAME is best understood as a landscape reference: it is the natural reference for whole-head and whole-face modelling rather than a direct solution to sparse nasal editing.
This contrast is useful.
FLAME shows that interpretable, disentangled control is a mature principle in face modelling, while Rhinoform's target is a local surgical-aesthetic subregion.
The editable and evaluated object is restricted to the nasal ROI so that the task remains local, morphology-focused and accountable at the nasal sub-unit level.

FaceScape provides the registered substrate for this project and is therefore another load-bearing reference.
It is a large-scale, high-quality, topologically uniform 3D face dataset with a detailed riggable prediction system ().

Its uniform topology is precisely what makes a fixed nasal ROI and a fixed landmark protocol meaningful: dense per-vertex error can be computed by direct index correspondence rather than by approximate surface matching.
The same property also allows nasal sub-units such as the radix, dorsum, tip and alar regions to be evaluated with fixed vertex sets across identities.

The relevance to the present work is therefore this: FaceScape supplies exactly the indexable topology that required to turn dense per-vertex error and the edge strain of Equation eq:edge-strain into exact quantities, while global face spaces such as 3DMM and FLAME capture plausible whole-face variation but are not tailored to local, sparse-control nasal editing.
Rhinoform resolves this mismatch by taking the data-aware coordinate system from statistical face modelling while rejecting global coefficient editing as the user-facing deformation mechanism.
This gap between global statistical priors and local handle-driven editing motivates the geometry-based deformation methods examined next.

Where statistical face models edit an entire face through global coefficients, classical interactive shape editing takes the opposite stance: move a few handles and propagate the deformation smoothly over the surface using a purely geometric energy.
These operators are transparent, data-agnostic baselines against which any data-aware nasal method must justify itself.

Rhinoform adopts three of the most representative members of this family---Laplacian editing, Bi-Laplacian editing and As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) editing---as external comparators, while using radial-basis-function (RBF) interpolation as a further landscape reference for sparse-handle dense-field interpolation.
These operators occupy the geometric branch of .

Laplacian surface editing represents a mesh in differential (Laplacian) coordinates: each vertex is encoded relative to its one-ring neighbourhood, and an edited surface is reconstructed by satisfying handle and anchor constraints while preserving those local details in a least-squares sense ().
Its input is a region of interest plus displaced handles and anchors; its output is a detail-preserving edited mesh; and its mechanism is a single sparse linear solve.
This is exactly the operator instantiated by Rhinoform's Laplacian geometric baseline.
Laplacian is a domain-relevant comparator because prior rhinoplasty planning work used volumetric Laplacian deformation, as detailed in .

The order of the smoothness energy matters. contrasts a first-order membrane energy, which minimises stretching and yields a C^0 surface with a visible crease at the handle, against a second-order Bi-Laplacian thin-plate energy, which minimises bending and yields a smoother C^1 surface .
Rhinoform includes both first- and second-order variants because this order trades local fidelity against global smoothness in a way that must be measured rather than assumed.

A smoother surface is not automatically a better nasal preview: excessive smoothing can suppress identity-specific or sub-unit-specific responses, while insufficient smoothing can introduce visible local artefacts.
The two variants therefore test different points on the same sparse-control propagation problem.
As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) editing takes a nonlinear route.
It seeks a deformation whose local one-ring cells stay as close to rigid as possible, alternately estimating a per-cell rotation and solving for vertex positions ().
This makes ARAP prized for artefact-resistant, regular surfaces, and it serves as the strongly regular geometric endpoint of the accuracy--regularity trade-off studied later.
RBF interpolation provides a further scattered-data alternative: it maps sparse handle displacements to a dense field through closed-form smoothness .

In this chapter RBF is kept as a landscape reference, showing that sparse-handle dense interpolation is a broader family than Laplacian and ARAP alone, while the main empirical comparison focuses on the most representative geometric editing operators.

The defining property of this family---and also its limitation---is that it is data-agnostic.

Geometry-based operators encode generic smoothness, bending or rigidity priors; they do not encode knowledge of how real noses vary across identities, nor how the radix, dorsum, tip and alar regions tend to move together under clinically meaningful edits.
They are therefore natural and necessary baselines for sparse-control nasal deformation, but not complete solutions to face-specific preview.

Their role in Rhinoform is diagnostic: they define the transparent regularity end of the design space against which a data-aware anchor and a learned residual correction must justify their added complexity.
The remedy considered next is to replace, or at least supplement, the generic geometric prior with a learned population prior.
A complementary line replaces the generic smoothness prior with a learned one.
The variational autoencoder (VAE) learns a latent generative model p_ (y ) together with an amortised inference network q_ (z ), trained by maximising an evidence lower bound.
Its conditional variant (CVAE) conditions both the prior and the generator on a side input x, so it can model a structured output distribution p_ (y ) rather than an unconditional one ().

Read as a network, the encoder maps an input y (and condition x) to a Gaussian latent described by and ; the reparameterisation z= + makes sampling differentiable; the decoder reconstructs y from (x,z); and a KL term regularises the latent towards the conditional prior.

In the mesh-deformation setting such models promise population-informed edits rather than purely smooth interpolation, and convolutional mesh autoencoders such as CoMA show that nonlinear mesh models can represent full-face expression manifolds with impressive fidelity.

The encoder q_ (z ,y) maps the input and condition to a Gaussian latent, the reparameterisation z= _ + _ makes sampling differentiable, and the decoder p_ (x ,y) reconstructs the output under a KL prior term.

In Rhinoform a CVAE-style generator is used only to correct a statistical anchor with a nonlinear residual, admitted under explicit geometric budgets, because an unconditioned generator drifts off-manifold near the edit boundary.
For sparse-control nasal editing, CVAE expressiveness cuts both ways.

Conditioned on sparse controls and trained on limited identities, a high-capacity generator can fit the training manifold while drifting near the boundaries of plausible edits, producing confident but degenerate surfaces.
Rhinoform therefore uses the CVAE as a nonlinear residual on top of a strong statistical anchor, with admission controlled by explicit geometric budgets.
The method chapter formalises this residual role, and the evaluation tests the direct-generator alternative.
The distinction between tasks is essential.
CoMA-style mesh autoencoding asks how well a model can compress or regenerate a full face/expression manifold without user handles.
Rhinoform asks a different question: after sparse anatomical controls have already fixed much of the low-frequency deformation, what residual dense ROI motion remains predictable and safe?
A neural result in the first regime does not automatically settle the second.

The global-edit limitation identified in is not unique to this project; it has driven a dedicated research line on localized 3DMM control that the survey of Egger et al.\ identifies as a central open problem of morphable-model research .

Early solutions localise a linear space directly: region-based linear face models split the face into independently controlled segments blended at their boundaries ; sparse localized deformation components (SPLOCS) impose spatial sparsity on the learned basis itself so that each component moves one coherent surface patch ; and anatomically-constrained local models attach patch-level shape subspaces to an underlying bone structure .
These works establish the principle Rhinoform also relies on: locality must be built into the representation, not recovered post hoc from a global basis.
A second generation makes the localized space neural.

Spiral convolutional networks (Neural3DMM) replace PCA with graph convolutions on a fixed mesh topology , and the Locally Adaptive Morphable Model (LAMM) is, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end framework in which displacements of a sparse set of control vertices directly steer a dense mesh output in a single forward pass, trained self-supervised by using sparse displacements to transform one training sample into another .

LAMM demonstrates strong disentanglement of the manipulated region from the preserved remainder and real-time inference on a single CPU thread---properties that make it the published method closest in spirit to the sparse-to-dense task studied here.

ShapeFusion replaces the regression view with a masked diffusion prior: a user selects an arbitrary manipulation region and an arbitrary set of handle vertices, and the model inpaints the masked region with diverse, plausible completions while exactly preserving unedited geometry .
Notably, its authors motivate exactly the application family Rhinoform targets---fine face-sculpting control---and demonstrate localized manipulation without predefined regions or control sets.
A third strand abandons the fixed mesh entirely.

Neural parametric head models (NPHM) represent identity as a signed-distance field composed of an ensemble of local MLPs anchored at facial keypoints, with expressions as a forward deformation field .

ImHead scales this implicit, localized programme to a corpus of roughly 4,000 identities and introduces a region-specific intermediate latent so that a compact global identity code can still support local edits of individual facial features, explicitly including nose-region manipulation .
Together these works show that localized, region-controllable editing is the current frontier of statistical head modelling, in both explicit-mesh and implicit form.
This frontier is engaged directly rather than deferred.

Following examiner feedback recommending comparison against this research line, LAMM---the member of the family whose task contract is closest to the present benchmark, since its sparse control-vertex displacements steer a dense mesh output in one forward pass---was retrained from scratch on the identity-disjoint split, with its manipulation patches instantiated as the five nasal sub-units and the nine benchmark landmarks supplied as its control set, and evaluated under the identical strict scorer on all 9\,900 held-out pairs ().

The result previews the central trade-off of this dissertation: LAMM attains the lowest reconstruction error of any evaluated method, while producing substantially more target-relative new normal flips and higher edge strain than the certified RB-SR operating point.
Two contract distinctions still bound what can be compared directly.

The representation contract: the per-vertex ROI error, sub-unit decomposition, edge-strain and normal-flip audits of this dissertation require exact index correspondence on a fixed FaceScape topology; implicit models such as NPHM and ImHead deliberately trade this correspondence away for topological freedom, so any comparison must pass through mesh extraction and non-rigid registration, which injects a correspondence error that is not attributable to the deformation mechanism itself.
ShapeFusion, as a stochastic diffusion inpainter, additionally requires a sampling-budget convention before its outputs are commensurable with deterministic predictors.

The safety contract: none of these systems expose a calibrated admission boundary---an instrumented notion of when a requested edit should be shrunk or refused--- because avatar editing does not need one, while a consultation preview does.

NPHM, ImHead and ShapeFusion are therefore specified as the next tier of external baselines under the bridging protocols of , while LAMM already serves as the measured accuracy frontier inside the benchmark.
A final research line must be acknowledged because it bounds what the certified admission stage of can claim as new.

Inversion-aware mesh deformation is an established topic in geometry processing: locally injective mappings (LIM) optimise deformation energies subject to a barrier that guarantees no element inverts ; scalable variants construct provably inversion-free simplicial maps ; and scalable locally injective mappings (SLIM) extend these guarantees to large meshes with robust reweighting .
On the learned side, Neural Jacobian Fields predict per-element Jacobians and recover the map by a differentiable Poisson solve, so that a geometric solver post-processes a learned field .
These works establish that inversion-aware optimisation, dedicated geometric solvers layered after learning, and learned deformation fields are each individually well known.
The specific construction of this dissertation is therefore deliberately narrow: RB-SR does not optimise a globally or locally injective map and does not guarantee an inversion-free surface.

Its certificate is anchor-relative---the admitted residual is attenuated until its folded faces are a subset of the ridge anchor's---which is a weaker statement chosen because it preserves a feasible real-time endpoint (the anchor itself) by construction.

What is specific to this work is the composition: a source-conditioned statistical anchor, a spatially gated learned residual, a hard anchor-relative fold certificate, and the binding of that exact composition into an auditable browser deployment. returns to the precise hierarchy of geometric statements this entitles.
Existing 3D aesthetic preview tools already establish the applied space.
The relevant related-work question is which deformation mechanisms are visible in the public record, and which parts of the sparse-control deformation problem remain untested.
Existing systems can be classified both by deployment category and by deformation mechanism.
Mechanistically, 2D photo morphing is accessible and visually persuasive but lacks a registered 3D surface and cannot expose local mesh regularity.
Manual 3D sculpting and slider-based morphing can support consultation but often depend on operator skill or proprietary deformation rules.
Template/anatomical generators and image-level generative models can produce appealing outcomes but are hard to audit as geometry.

Finite-element or biomechanical simulation is the physically richer route, but it requires anatomical layers, material assumptions and patient-specific calibration far beyond the registered surface dataset used here.

Laplacian, ARAP and FFD/RBF-style control-point deformation offer transparent sparse-control geometry, but they are data-agnostic. 3DMM/PCA statistical models are transparent and data-aware, but their linear residual boundary must be measured.

Rhinoform deliberately sits between these categories: more geometric than 2D morphing, more transparent than black-box simulators, lighter than FEM, more controllable than image-level generation, more data-aware than pure Laplacian/ARAP editing, and safer than an unconditional neural generator.
Commercial capture and planning platforms, including Canfield VECTRA, MirrorMe3D, 3dMDvultus and LifeViz, establish 3D consultation, measurement and monitoring as mature workflows .
Consumer and SDK-facing preview tools, including Crisalix, Banuba, FaceTouchUp, AEDIT and Arbrea, demonstrate demand for interactive visual reshaping and accessible before/after communication .
Their internal deformation algorithms are generally proprietary, so they are treated here as motivating systems rather than as reproducible baselines.
Academic and open-source systems provide a clearer view of mechanism.
Digitizing Rhinoplasty uses a web workflow for 3D preoperative evaluation with extensive landmark marking and automatic facial measurement, evaluated with surgeon feedback .
RhinOnBlender offers a free 3D rhinoplasty planning add-on in open-source software .

The baselines used later also have a direct clinical precedent: an established rhinoplasty planning and simulation system is built on volumetric Laplacian differential-surface deformation, driven by sparse sketch contours and clinically validated against post-operative CT .
This is direct evidence that Laplacian-family handle deformation is a documented operating mechanism for nasal-surface editing rather than an arbitrary comparator.

It also marks the boundary this project respects: that system models calibrated volumetric soft tissue from patient CT, whereas the present work deliberately stays at uncalibrated surface morphology on a shared FaceScape topology.

The two are therefore not evaluated on a common benchmark; the contribution here is to test the same Laplacian mechanism under a controlled identity-level protocol, not to reproduce a clinical CT simulation.
Other structured-light and rule-based simulation systems combine keypoints, aesthetic indices and mesh-morphing operators with quantitative evaluation or standardised manoeuvres .
Landmark-driven generative pipelines such as LandmarkDiff shift the mechanism toward image generation from dense landmarks .

These examples motivate the baseline families used later: geometric propagation for transparent handle editing, statistical sparse-to-dense regression for data-aware mesh response, and learned residuals for nonlinear correction.

They also clarify the project boundary: if a system outputs an image-level prediction rather than a registered mesh deformation, it may be visually persuasive but cannot be audited directly through per-vertex ROI error, normal flips or edge strain.

A recent systematic review of simulation and AI in rhinoplasty identifies a recurring methodological weakness: the absence of an automated evaluation method and a heavy reliance on subjective surgeon feedback .
This is the gap a controlled sparse-to-dense benchmark addresses.

Existing tools overwhelmingly emphasise visualisation, measurement, planning or photorealistic prediction; the missing element is a controlled, identity-level benchmark that asks which deformation family is trustworthy for sparse-control editing, together with an interface that surfaces the resulting credibility limits to the user.
For that reason, the evidence used for external-tool positioning must be tiered honestly.
This project has no local, instrumented access to any competitor product, so nothing in is a head-to-head measurement.
The comparison is deliberately qualitative positioning drawn from vendor materials and peer-reviewed reviews.

Three evidence tiers are kept distinct: measured in this work means the sparse-to-dense accuracy, regularity, sub-unit and robustness numbers computed under one FaceScape protocol in ; supported by public materials means that commercial tools exist, are adopted in consultation and emphasise visualisation, capture accuracy or physical guides; and qualitative positioning only means that any statement that this project's deformation model is more auditable than a competitor's is a claim about published emphasis, not a benchmark result, because competitors' deformation internals are proprietary and were never run here.

The positioning is therefore empirical where it can be and conservative where it must be.
Laplacian and ARAP in this dissertation are representative geometric families, not claims about the hidden implementation of any commercial product.

The contribution is to make the deformation model, risk metrics, refusal boundary and evaluation protocol explicit and reproducible in a space whose public evidence is dominated by visualisation and capture.
Read together, the surveyed strands each supply one ingredient the platform needs and each leave one requirement unmet.
It is the combination of the unmet requirements that defines the contribution.

The statistical face models of ---3DMM, its PCA shape space and FLAME---contribute a registered, data-aware coordinate system but edit globally, so they do not deliver the local, handle-driven control that the consultation setting demands.

The geometry-based operators of ---Laplacian, Bi-Laplacian and ARAP---contribute transparent sparse-handle control, but their data-agnostic priors are accurate only up to a generic smoothness assumption.

The learning-based models of contribute a population-aware prior that can capture nonlinear population-level nasal morphology response, but a direct conditional generator can drift off-manifold at the edit boundary where the tool is most used.

The localized neural morphable models of ---LAMM, ShapeFusion, NPHM and ImHead---contribute region-controllable neural shape spaces and confirm that localized editing is where the field is moving; LAMM, evaluated inside the benchmark, indeed sets the measured accuracy frontier, but the family is built for generative avatar editing and carries no calibrated admission or refusal boundary, and its measured accuracy is bought with markedly higher fold and strain incidence ().

Finally, the consultation and commercial systems of confirm strong demand for interactive 3D preview yet, as the systematic reviews note, are dominated by visualisation and capture rather than a reproducible, risk-instrumented deformation benchmark.

The resulting gap is precise: to the best of our knowledge, no publicly reported prior tool couples a controlled FaceScape nasal sparse-control deformation benchmark to a limitation-aware interactive prototype with live geometric and distributional risk gates.
This dissertation addresses that gap through a benchmark-calibrated prototype that exposes control-applicability, edge-strain and normal-flip instruments.
The control-applicability policy can scale back or withhold edits outside the evaluated control envelope; the geometric instruments remain read-outs.

The prototype is designed from the consultation setting outward.
A patient and a surgeon need a nasal preview that is credible, interpretable and explicit about its risk boundary.
The design goals below therefore map each interface decision to benchmark evidence, rather than presenting the prototype as a generic list of features.
The default state of the tool is the Ridge anchor.
This choice serves the first requirement of consultation use: the interface should respond immediately and retain a deterministic preview while the learned refinement is computed.
The evaluation justifies this anchor-first contract in ; the prototype makes the active layer and every transition away from it explicit.
The learned residual is therefore a proposal, not an unconditional output: it replaces the anchor only after exact handles have been re-imposed and the Ridge-relative fold certificate has completed.
The interface separates two kinds of runtime evidence.
Control applicability is computed from the requested 27-dimensional edit and can retain, scale back or withhold the request.
Geometric read-outs such as anchor normal flips and edge-strain p_95 describe the displayed mesh, while certificate status, residual retention and projection rounds describe the learned refinement.
These quantities are not merged into a confidence score or clinical-safety claim.
The prototype keeps the full-head mesh as the viewing context while organising control and feedback in nasal sub-unit language.
Patient complaints often localise to the dorsum, tip and alae, but those local changes need to be viewed in the context of the whole face to remain meaningful ().

The interface also states the system boundary explicitly: the current mesh uses uncalibrated FaceScape units and a single expression, so the prototype is intended for morphology communication rather than surgical-outcome prediction (). collects these design goals as a requirement-to-evidence index; the table is a navigation aid, while the rationale is given in the surrounding text.

Its visible controls---tip rotation, tip projection, dorsum height, alar width, bridge smoothing and tip width---are a human-facing wrapper around the same nine-landmark sparse-control protocol defined in .

At runtime the browser first assigns anatomical roles to the nine registered landmark vertices using their position in the registered ROI: the most anterior landmark is the tip, the most superior landmark is the radix, the two most lateral landmarks are the alae, and the remaining central landmarks form the dorsum group.
Each semantic slider then writes signed displacements into selected entries of the 27-dimensional control vector c=[ x_1, y_1, z_1, , x_9, y_9, z_9].
The sidebar is deliberately limited to these six controls.

They span nasal changes that can be expressed cleanly by the available nine handles---tip rotation about the alar-base pivot, tip anterior--posterior projection, central dorsum height, bilateral alar width, source-adaptive dorsal-profile smoothing and tip-lobule width---without pretending that the prototype can model every surgical manoeuvre.

Adding more sliders would create a false sense of precision unless each new control could be mapped to a stable subset of the same nine landmarks and governed by the same applicability and certificate contracts.
The six-control design is therefore a constraint, not a missing feature: it keeps the interface aligned with the benchmarked sparse-control problem and avoids unvalidated free-form vertex sculpting.

The first is input applicability: after every edit the browser computes the control-scale statistic (c) = _k (c_k/ _k)^2, where the per-coordinate scales _k are estimated from the validation controls and then fixed.
Requests with 7.4921 pass unchanged; requests with 7.4921 < 9.3966 are scaled back; requests with > 9.3966 are withheld.
This statistic is a statement about the evaluated control range, not a calibrated out-of-distribution probability.
The second mechanism is the ridge-relative fold certificate of , which governs whether the learned residual may replace the anchor at all.
Neither mechanism is presented to the user as ``safety'' or ``confidence''.

Exposing the residual this way is not a presentation choice; it fixes three properties that the method in is then obliged to satisfy.
First, the displayed layer is non-destructive: research mode can inspect Auto, Anchor or Certified, while Auto keeps the anchor until a certified result is available.
The method therefore produces a correction defined relative to the anchor, \, R_ in , so retaining the anchor never requires a second solve.
Second, the instrument deliberately exposes no global ``residual strength'' control.

A single scalar would let a proposal that lowers average error still open fold-over in one sub-unit while another stays untouched, and the gate state in would then have to reject the entire edit rather than the offending region.

The runtime instead demands admission that is decided per region, which is precisely the constraint that forces the method away from the global- Hybrid and towards the per-vertex admission weight g(v) of ; the spatial structure that makes this necessary is diagnosed in .
Third, the learned gate and the non-learned certificate must be reproducible from the current browser state.
The gate uses the inference inputs specified in ; orientation and strain budgets supervise it during training but are not additional feed-forward inputs.
Exact handles are then re-imposed, and the iterative certificate checks the resulting raw field against the Ridge fold set.
The interface reports the certificate result rather than presenting gate output as a probability of correctness.
One honesty question must be settled explicitly: is the smooth geometry the user sees the same geometry the benchmark scores?
The answer is deliberately no, and the separation is engineered rather than incidental.

For display, the browser subtracts the zero-control anchor field, tapers the edit towards the ROI boundary along graph-geodesic distance, and applies a small number of rim-pinned Laplacian smoothing rounds so that the edited nose sits seamlessly in the full-face render; the certified overlay additionally fills one-ring landmark residuals before smoothing.

None of these display transforms touches the evaluation frame: the raw inference path first re-imposes the nine hard handles exactly, then runs the fold certificate, and only afterwards hands the geometry to the display pipeline.
The strict scorer of operates exclusively on the pre-display geometry.

This prevents a cosmetic smoothing pass from silently substituting for the stricter benchmark geometry---and it is itself verified: the released browser build is locked to the released assets by content hash and passes 51 automated checks against stored reference goldens, with a worst-case certified-path vertex deviation of 5.4 10^-7 model units ().
The prototype is bounded by design.

A mandatory disclaimer banner states that it is a research prototype and not a medical device; that coordinates are uncalibrated FaceScape units; and that outputs are for morphology communication only.
It is technically evaluated, not clinically validated---no user study is claimed, and a formative study would require the appropriate institutional ethics decision ().
These boundaries are surfaced in the interface, not buried in a manual, because explicit scoping is part of what makes the instrument trustworthy.
The scope statement also fixes the terms in which the method is allowed to optimise.

Because the working units are uncalibrated and relative, every quantity the method minimises or budgets---the dense target of , and the orientation and edge-strain budgets that constrain g(v)---is defined in those same relative units, so no absolute metric claim about a patient's nose is derivable from the output and none is reported.

Equally, the interface does not translate an applicability breach into a confidence claim: a near-boundary request is visibly scaled to the evaluated boundary, and an outside-range request is withheld.
For requests that remain applicable, the learned correction is displayed only after the separate Ridge-relative fold certificate.
The responsible-use boundary is therefore implemented in the runtime contract rather than added only as explanatory text.

The RB-SR framework (residual-based safety refinement) is a certificate-guarded residual deformation pipeline with four stages.
Ridge regression serves as the stable sparse-to-dense backbone: it provides the first dense estimate and the fallback state.
A residual model proposes local nonlinear corrections.
A learned per-vertex gate admits those corrections spatially.

Finally, a hard ridge-relative fold certificate projects the admitted residual so that the folded faces of the output are a subset of the anchor's---a deployment contract that, as shows, soft optimisation alone failed to provide.

The prototype therefore deploys only the two methods with distinct interaction value: Ridge as the immediate real-time editor and fallback, and certified RB-SR as the main personalised enhanced preview. summarises the end-to-end protocol the rest of this chapter follows, read left to right: an identity-disjoint FaceScape split feeds independent method lanes, all lanes are scored on one common evidence battery, and every comparison is resolved by identity-level paired inference before the whole procedure is released under a single reproducibility guarantee.
The chapter's narrative is deliberately staged, and each stage carries an explicit evidence tier.
Primary evidence is the PCA-64 held-out test protocol, unlocked exactly once on the 9\,900 held-out pairs; it supports every headline claim.
Validation evidence is used for component diagnosis and operating-point selection before held-out evaluation.
Post-hoc evidence---the PCA-128 capacity study and the diagnostic breakdowns---was produced after the primary analysis and can generate hypotheses but cannot strengthen confirmatory claims.
Supplementary evidence covers conformance and reproducibility checks on the released artefacts.

The staging of the results follows the same logic: certified RB-SR is first placed against the classical and direct-generation baselines (), then against the strong learned baseline LAMM (), then the post-hoc PCA-128 study asks what changes when anchor capacity is unlocked (), and only then is the overall accuracy--regularity trade-off adjudicated ().

All comparisons in this chapter run on the benchmark instantiation of the sparse-control dense-deformation task formalised in : ordered source--target identity pairs supply a measurable dense target, the nine landmark displacements act as hard controls, and scoring is restricted to the free ROI vertices.

This section fixes the remaining experimental contract --- the held-out data split, the compared methods, the metric set and the statistical decision rule --- so that every later result is read against one fixed protocol.

FaceScape is used because its registered topology makes the per-vertex error and risk metrics exact by index correspondence (), and it provides enough identities to run an identity-disjoint, all-pairs evaluation protocol instead of cherry-picked edits.
The dataset construction starts from 847 FaceScape identities.
One identity (subject 832) lacks a usable neutral-expression mesh and is removed, leaving 846 valid identities in the parent pool.
For the final confirmation rerun, the 100 identities in the previously observed parent test set are first excluded, leaving 746 eligible identities.

The frozen confirmation manifest then orders identities by ascending SHA256(schema \_id) with split\_seed=20260809 and assigns test, then validation, then training: 100 confirmation-test, 70 validation and 576 training identities.
This final split is therefore hash-ordered, not PCA-stratified.
It is fixed before confirmation training and is never re-drawn or tuned on confirmation-test performance.
No identity that appears as a source or target in the 9900 final test pairs occurs among the training or validation identities.

Any identity-level statistic used as a model input---in particular the 64-dimensional source-PCA code---is fit on the 576 training identities only, so the split is leakage-free at both the pair and feature level.
The final test set yields all 100 99=9900 ordered source--target pairs as the canonical strict evaluation set, and the validation set yields all 70 69=4830 ordered pairs.

One boundary of this design is declared rather than hidden: the 100 test identities are excluded from the final retrain, but they were not historically untouched during earlier development of the project, and no independent external test set exists.

The reported result is therefore internal identity-disjoint confirmatory evidence---stronger than a tuned validation number because the held-out test chain was unlocked exactly once, but one tier below external validation, and every claim in this dissertation is scoped to that tier ().
The ROI is partitioned into the five anatomical sub-units of .

This partition is essential for evaluation because average ROI RMSE and geometric risk do not localise to the same regions: root/dorsum are often accuracy-hard but flip-safe, while tip and alae carry much of the flip risk.
The compared methods cover three roles.

External baselines are faithful re-implementations of deformation mechanisms already established in the nasal-editing and 3D-face literature surveyed in (Laplacian and bi-Laplacian , ARAP , CVAE-only , and the localized neural 3DMM editor LAMM , retrained from scratch on the identity-disjoint training split).
They are run under the identical ROI topology, control encoding and metric set as the proposed methods.

Because no prior system has been evaluated on this FaceScape sparse-control protocol, they stand for documented mechanisms, not for the published results of any specific system, so the comparison is mechanism-level by design.

The matched internal reference and ablations are the ridge-only reference, hybrid residual and gate variants: they explain why the proposed method has an anchor, a residual proposal and an admission layer.
The proposed operating point is certified RB-SR, with the ridge anchor as its conservative fallback.
Why exactly these five external baselines.
Each baseline is a faithful re-implementation of one deformation principle that the related-work survey () identifies as a way to turn sparse handles into a dense ``after'' nose.

Together they span the field's three paradigms---classical geometric propagation, direct neural generation, and localized neural shape-space editing---and bracket the accuracy/regularity plane, so that any win by the proposed method cannot be attributed to a missing or straw-man comparator.
Each is a fair comparator because it is run under the identical ROI topology, identity split, control encoding and metric set as RB-SR; the only thing that varies is the deformation mechanism.

All five appear in the headline benchmark () and the sub-unit decomposition (); the noise-robustness study () focuses on the decision-relevant quartet (anchor, certified RB-SR, LAMM, ARAP); the classical baselines keep their own diagnostic packs in ; and the LAMM comparison receives its own staged analysis in .
Represents the membrane/minimal-surface tradition of sparse-handle mesh editing .
It is a fair comparator because it is the canonical way to diffuse a few landmark displacements smoothly across a surface.
In the evaluation it tests whether a generic smoothness prior is sufficient for face-specific nasal response.
Represents the thin-plate/curvature-minimising end of the same family.
It is included to test the intuition that a smoother field is automatically a safer or more faithful nasal preview.
The evaluation measures that assumption directly through RMSE, normal-flip and edge-strain metrics.
Represents the shape-preserving, detail-retaining end of geometry processing .
It is the conservative geometric comparator: if a method improves accuracy by allowing non-rigid residuals, ARAP shows the regularity cost against a strong local-rigidity prior.
Represents the recent move to generate the dense ``after'' shape directly with a deep conditional model , with no linear anchor.
It is the essential learning baseline because it tests the direct-generator alternative to an anchored pipeline.
Its role is to separate the value of learned capacity from the value of source-conditioned anchoring and residual admission.
Represents the state-of-the-art localized shape-space frontier surveyed in , and is included following examiner feedback recommending a comparison against this research line.

Because its published checkpoint is trained on a different corpus, LAMM is retrained from scratch on the identity-disjoint split, with its manipulation patches instantiated as the five nasal sub-units and the nine benchmark landmarks supplied as its control set, and evaluated under the identical strict scorer.
It is the strong accuracy comparator: it asks whether a modern region-controllable mesh autoencoder simply dominates the anchored pipeline.
The remaining members of the localized-editing family---ShapeFusion's masked diffusion editor and the implicit localized head models NPHM and ImHead ---are acknowledged but not run in this round.

Their obstacle is representational: the implicit models abandon the fixed topology on which the index-exact metrics depend, so a faithful comparison requires a registration bridge whose error would contaminate the scorer, and ShapeFusion requires a sampling-budget convention for its stochastic outputs. specifies the adaptation protocol under which each becomes commensurable; with LAMM already measured, these remain the next tier rather than the first.

This section settles the first stage: how does the certified pipeline fare against the classical geometric editors, the direct neural generator, and its matched internal reference and residual ablation?
The strong learned baseline LAMM appears in for completeness---the table is a single committed artefact---but its analysis is deliberately deferred to .

The predeclared primary hypothesis of the entire evaluation is intentionally modest and internal: certified RB-SR must beat its own matched ridge anchor on ROI RMSE without increasing target-relative new flips, with the certificate holding on every pair.
That hypothesis passes: RMSE falls from 1.0739 to 1.0599 (-1.30\%) and new flips fall from 0.332\% to 0.227\% (-31.6\%), with the fold-subset certificate satisfied on all 9\,900 pairs.

On registered FaceScape topology every identity shares a vertex indexing, so per-vertex RMSE is the exact, correspondence-aware error; Chamfer/nearest-neighbour distances are unnecessary here because they discard the known correspondence and are strictly less informative.
We report uncalibrated FaceScape units rather than millimetres, consistent with .

ROI RMSE here measures how faithfully the learned sparse-to-dense map reconstructs the dense nasal deformation of unseen identities, i.e.\ whether the population-level control shape regularity generalises rather than overfits.

Against the external comparators of this stage, certified RB-SR at ROI RMSE 1.0599 is 35\% lower than Laplacian (1.6420), 38\% lower than ARAP (1.6969), 47\% lower than bi-Laplacian (2.0071) and 20\% lower than the direct CVAE generator (1.3195), while simultaneously recording fewer target-relative new flips than any of them except ARAP.

Two readings of the non-LAMM rows drive the rest of the chapter.

First, the geometric editors are regular but not accurate: ARAP is the best method on both regularity columns (lowest edge-strain and lowest flips), yet its ROI RMSE is 60\% higher than certified RB-SR's.
A generic smoothness/rigidity prior can move vertices cleanly but does not know how a specific nose should respond to a sparse edit.

Second, the direct CVAE generator is the opposite extreme: its flexibility is in fact more accurate than every geometric baseline (ROI RMSE 1.3195 vs.\ 1.6420--2.0071), confirming a learned map captures dense response generic geometry misses---but it pays with far worse regularity (1.352\% flips), so an unconstrained nonlinear generator is not the answer either.
Each prior is strong on one axis and weak on the other.

That certified RB-SR does not win every column---ARAP legitimately wins regularity, and LAMM will be seen to win raw accuracy---is deliberate evidence that the metric set is the field-standard ``accuracy + geometric regularity'' pairing applied identically to all methods, not a set tuned to flatter the proposed method.

The geometric-propagation family (Laplacian, bi-Laplacian, ARAP) represents the smoothness/rigidity mesh-editing tradition that also underlies volumetric-Laplacian surgical planners such as Liao's ; the CVAE represents the recent move toward directly generating the ``after'' shape with deep generative models ; and LAMM represents the localized neural shape-space frontier of .
The benchmark therefore spans the main families identified in related work under one controlled protocol.
They are faithful re-implementations of deformation mechanisms (); they are not the commercial or clinical systems of .
Systems such as VECTRA, Crisalix, Liao's planner and Topsakal's web tool use different data, metrics and (often calibrated) units, so no system-level numeric comparison is possible.
The comparison here is therefore deliberately mechanism-level and protocol-controlled, which is precisely the gap identified in .
Design consequence for Rhinoform.
The headline confirms, at the level of the full external comparison, what the derivation already argued mechanism-by-mechanism: there is no single hidden ``best render''.

Generic geometry is too inaccurate and a free neural generator too unstable; what the platform needs, and what the derivation produced, is an auditable, data-aware anchor with a controlled residual correction on top.
The next section proves that this derived object is also the best deployable operating point.
The per-baseline distributional evidence supports three method-level readings, with the consolidated spatial and regional-tail comparison in .

ARAP provides the strongest regularity endpoint among the external geometric baselines, with the lowest incidence of newly introduced normal flips and comparatively restrained edge distortion; its regional error nevertheless remains consistently elevated, showing that geometric regularity alone does not recover the identity-specific dense nasal deformation the personalised sparse-to-dense task requires.

Bi-Laplacian propagation shows that increasing smoothness does not improve either accuracy or geometric safety: it is dominated by the other geometric baselines on aggregate error, and its regional and tail profiles localise severe distortions to the high-curvature nasal sub-units, ruling it out as either a prediction method or a regularity-oriented fallback.

Laplacian propagation sits between the two: markedly more stable than bi-Laplacian and free of its worst tail failures, but with regional error well above the data-aware methods---a useful identity-agnostic middle baseline that cannot infer the dense, source-specific nasal response from sparse landmark controls.

LAMM attains the lowest ROI RMSE of any evaluated method (0.9715 against certified RB-SR's 1.0599, a +0.0884 deficit for RB-SR that the paired procedure resolves decisively in LAMM's favour, Holm-adjusted p 3.9 10^-16).

Three consequences follow.

First, the accuracy frontier of this task is now measured, not conjectured: a modern region-controllable mesh autoencoder does reconstruct held-out nasal deformation more accurately than the anchored linear-plus-residual pipeline, and the dissertation reports that plainly.

Second, accuracy is not the axis on which LAMM would be deployed: its flip and strain behaviour is worse than every anchored configuration, and it exposes no fallback anchor, no admission boundary and no fold certificate, so its extra accuracy arrives without any of the machinery that argued a consultation preview requires.

Third, the comparison raises a fair question the staged narrative must answer before adjudicating the trade-off: is RB-SR's accuracy deficit intrinsic to the certified architecture, or an artefact of the deliberately rationed anchor capacity?
That is the question the post-hoc capacity study addresses next.
The stage-wise validation evidence is reported with the method derivation in ; the capacity question can therefore be asked here about the correct component without repeating the selection evidence.

This section carries the post-hoc evidence tier defined in , and every claim in it is bounded accordingly: the study was designed after the primary test unlock, so it can generate hypotheses about capacity but cannot strengthen or replace the PCA-64 primary analysis.

The study holds the 9\,900 test pairs, strict scorer and LAMM outputs fixed, but changes several RB-SR components: the source basis grows from PCA-64 to PCA-128 with the ridge penalty re-selected on validation ( =1), a deterministic proposer replaces the CVAE, and the gate calibration is re-selected on the validation set.
The resulting certified RB-SR point records ROI RMSE 0.9153, new flips 0.7934\% and edge-strain p_95 0.2996---better than the LAMM on all three headline metrics (0.9715, 0.8787\%, 0.3196).

Exploratory paired comparisons clustered separately by source and target identity pass the stored Holm-corrected three-metric procedure, but that correction does not account for the capacity search that preceded the study, which is precisely why the result is labelled post-hoc.
Two readings keep the result honest.
First, the operating point is effectively anchor-dominated: the PCA-128 gate has a mean admission of only 0.0021 and no vertex exceeds 0.5.
The study therefore supports a capacity-oriented hypothesis: a stronger anchor family can move the certified pipeline toward or beyond LAMM's accuracy frontier.
Because , the proposer and gate calibration also change, it does not isolate PCA dimension as the sole causal factor.
Second, the higher-capacity point changes the regularity trade-off: new flips rise from the primary point's 0.227\% to 0.793\%.

The PCA-128 point is thus a different position on the same accuracy--regularity frontier, not a free upgrade---and the primary PCA-64 configuration remains the deployed, blind-confirmed operating point.

Gate activation is sparse, the admitted correction is local, and the final deformation remains close to the stable Ridge field.

This behaviour is consistent with the limited residual headroom established earlier: RB-SR is not required to replace the anchor with a free dense generator, but only to recover a small, predictable component of the remaining deformation.

Where that correction is admitted anatomically is shown by the Stage 3 mechanism map in : the pattern is selective rather than uniform, with stronger correction along parts of the dorsum--tip column and reduced admission across higher-risk lateral and alar regions.
Together, these diagnostics show that RB-SR's advantage does not come from replacing the anchor with a larger opaque generator.
It comes from combining a compact residual predictor with spatially selective admission.
The former estimates the limited recoverable correction, while the latter allocates that correction according to its predicted local benefit and geometric cost.
